fixes.answer: Music holds a unique and powerful place in human life. It has an extraordinary ability to [[evoke]] emotion, from joy to sorrow, and to comfort us in a way few other things can. It is also deeply tied to memory and identity, and it brings people together, whether at concerts or festivals. In my view, music is a universal language that [[transcends]] barriers and speaks directly to our emotions, which is why it is so [[cherished]].

It has changed dramatically. In the past, people bought physical records or CDs and often listened to a whole album deliberately. Now, streaming gives us instant access to virtually all recorded music, and we tend to consume it in playlists and individual tracks. This is wonderfully convenient, but some argue it has made listening more [[passive]] and [[fragmented]]. So access has expanded enormously, but our engagement with music may have become more [[cursory]].

Learning an instrument has remarkably positive effects. Many believe it enhances cognitive development, improving skills like memory, concentration and mathematical ability. It also teaches discipline, patience and perseverance, since [[mastery]] requires consistent practice. Furthermore, it provides a creative outlet and a real sense of accomplishment that boosts confidence. So beyond the joy of making music, it offers profound [[developmental]] and [[character-building]] benefits.

I believe the arts are absolutely vital, though often [[undervalued]]. They enrich our lives, [[provoke thought]], and allow us to explore and express the full range of human experience. The arts preserve culture and history, foster empathy by exposing us to different perspectives, and can even drive social change. Economically, the creative industries are significant too. So far from being a luxury, the arts are, in my view, essential to a civilised and [[reflective]] society.
fixes.why: 'essential' and 'society' are plain; marked 'undervalued' and 'provoke thought'

fixes.answer: Undoubtedly, and it already is. Technology is providing artists with powerful new tools and mediums, from digital art to AI-generated music, expanding creative possibilities. It has also democratised the arts, allowing anyone to create and share their work globally. However, this raises questions about [[authenticity]] and the role of human creativity. So while technology will transform and [[democratise]] the arts, I hope it will [[augment]] human expression rather than replace it.

Supporting the arts requires a [[multi-pronged]] approach. Governments should recognise their cultural and economic value and provide stable funding rather than treating them as [[expendable]]. Encouraging private sponsorship and [[philanthropy]] can supplement this. Integrating arts education properly into schools ensures future generations value them. Making the arts more accessible and affordable to ordinary people also builds public support. Essentially, we must treat the arts as an investment, not a luxury.

Certainly. Arts subjects develop invaluable skills like critical thinking, creativity, communication and empathy, which are highly transferable and increasingly prized by employers. They encourage us to [[grapple with]] complex human questions. The perceived disadvantage is that arts degrees are sometimes seen as less directly employable than sciences. However, I think this is often overstated, as the skills they cultivate are genuinely [[versatile]]. So both paths have distinct and equal [[merit]].
